title: The inner ruler
hookLine: the salt-and-banyan father of the Chandogya steps up as a challenger and hears of the one who lives inside everything, unseen
carry: the inner ruler lives in every being
tomorrow: Gargi stands up again with two questions like arrows. what are they?

cards: An old friend steps up. In the Chandogya, Uddalaka Aruni was the father who dropped salt in water and split a banyan seed for his son, and said: you are that.
Now he stands up in Janaka's court as a challenger, and like Bhujyu, he brings a question from a spirit.
Years ago, he says, a spirit speaking through a woman asked us: do you know the thread that strings this world, the next world and all beings together? Do you know the inner controller?
Yajnavalkya, if you drive off those cows without knowing them, your head will fall off.

teach.h: ANYONE CAN SAY I KNOW, I KNOW.
teach.b: I know them, Yajnavalkya says. Anyone can say I know, I know, says Uddalaka. Tell us.
The thread, says Yajnavalkya, is wind: like a string through beads, it holds this world and the next together. Then the inner controller, in a long chant.
He who lives in the earth, yet is other than the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body the earth is, who rules the earth from within: he is your self, the inner controller, the deathless.
Then the same lines for water, fire, the sun, all beings. Then it turns inward: the breath, the eye, the mind. And the close.
He is the unseen seer, the unheard hearer, the unthought thinker, the unknown knower. There is no other seer but him. And Uddalaka falls silent.

teach.h: THE INNER RULER LIVES IN EVERY BEING.
teach.b: This is the antaryamin, the inner ruler, one of the great Hindu pictures of the divine: not only above the world, but inside every part of it, nearer than the thing itself knows.
Ramanuja, the Vishishtadvaita teacher, took the phrase whose body the earth is and taught that the world and every soul are the body of God, who lives within them.
Shankara, the Advaita teacher, read the inner controller as the one self. Either way, the person in front of you has someone living in them they may never have noticed.
It's one way many Hindus explain namaste: folded hands for the one who lives inside the other.

how: The antaryamin passage is central in Sri Vaishnava theology, where God is understood as the inner ruler of all; students of other Vedanta schools study it too, and many Hindus explain the folded hands of namaste as honoring the divine within the other person.

o: the salt-and-seed father, now a challenger
the spirit who spoke through a woman
the king who offered the thousand cows

games.q: what's inside the answer — tap the pairs.
p: his body; it doesn't know him
the world as the body of God

s: in the passage, the earth knows its inner controller
he lives in the earth, and the earth does not know him.
Ramanuja built his teaching of the world as God's body on passages like this
whose body the earth is: a key phrase for Vishishtadvaita.
Uddalaka also appears in the Chandogya
as Shvetaketu's father, the teacher of you are that.

games.q: the inner controller lives in the earth, and the earth does not know him. what does that mean for a stranger you pass on the street?
o: the same inner ruler lives in them, unseen, whether they know it or not.
nothing; only holy people have an inner ruler.
only people who know about him have him inside.
games.why: he lives in all beings, and they don't know him. knowing isn't the condition; he's there either way.

practice: Feel the breath, and let the line come: lives in the breath, yet other than the breath. Then the resting eyes, then the mind with all its traffic: lives in it, yet the mind doesn't know it.
If you pray, fold your hands for a moment at the end; if not, just rest them. Notice whether something steady seems to sit under each of these, watching.

wordCard.voice: Uddalaka. The teacher who asked about the thread and the antaryamin, the inner controller: the one who lives in each thing, whom the thing doesn't know, and who rules it from within.

orig.note: Sanskrit antaryāmin: antar (within) + yam (to hold, to rule): the one who rules from within.

carryVoice: Your line: the inner ruler lives in every being. Tomorrow, Gargi comes back, with two questions like two arrows. Until then.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.12–13 (Uddalaka, the banyan seed and the salt)
Ramanuja, Sri Bhashya (the world as the body of Brahman)
